title: TCS and Infosys AI Revenue Crosses 10 Percent, Challenging SaaSpocalypse Fears
excerpt: TCS annualised AI revenue hit $3.1 billion and Infosys AI grew 29% in Q2 FY27, even as overall growth stayed modest and Infosys cut guidance to 1-2%.
body:
• AI passed 10% of revenue at both TCS and Infosys in the July-September quarter (Q2 FY27) for the first time.
  • TCS reported annualised AI revenue of $3.1 billion, up about 19% quarter on quarter; Infosys reported AI at 10.5% of revenue, up 29% quarter on quarter.
  • The Nifty IT index has risen more than 16% in October after falling 27% from January to early October, when SaaSpocalypse fears hit software and services stocks.
  • Caution remains: Infosys cut FY27 revenue guidance to 1-2%, and overall growth stayed modest — for investors, AI growth must still offset deflation in traditional work.

Artificial intelligence now accounts for more than a tenth of revenue at India's two largest IT services companies, September-quarter results show, undercutting the claim that AI agents would quickly make outsourcers and software firms obsolete — the fear markets labelled the SaaSpocalypse.

Tata Consultancy Services said annualised AI revenue reached $3.1 billion, crossing 10% of total revenue, with growth of more than 19% from the previous quarter. Infosys said AI made up 10.5% of revenue and grew 29% quarter on quarter. HCLTech, reporting a narrower advanced AI line, put that revenue at $219 million, up 28.4% sequentially.

From pilots to production budgets

The numbers mark a change in how enterprise AI is bought. Work that sat in proofs of concept is now funded as production programmes: data foundations, agentic workflows and modernisation tied to AI. Infosys also booked $5.2 billion in large-deal total contract value in the quarter, including a deal above $2 billion, according to reporting summarised by Elets CIO.

"As enterprises move to AI adoption at scale, the strong growth in AI revenues is a recognition of our differentiated market positioning and client confidence."

— Salil Parekh, CEO and Managing Director, Infosys

Market sentiment has followed the disclosures. The Nifty IT index is up more than 16% this month after a 27% fall from the start of the year to early October, and India's 24 listed IT services firms have added more than 31,000 jobs since April, according to Vallum Capital figures reported by the Financial Times via Dealroom. The industry generates about $300 billion and is India's largest white-collar employer.

The other side of the ledger

AI revenue does not settle the investment case. Overall growth stayed modest: TCS revenue rose 0.5% sequentially in constant currency, and Infosys cut its full-year FY27 guidance to 1% to 2%. TCS chief executive K. Krithivasan described a deflationary effect as AI productivity gains reduce the price clients pay for traditional, effort-based work, and said it was too early to call the end of that deflation.

Analysts also warn that AI revenue is defined by each company, not by a common standard, so cross-company comparisons carry limits. Part of the reported AI total may be existing work reclassified as it is rebuilt around AI, rather than entirely new spending. BNP Paribas analyst Kumar Rakesh has cautioned against assuming AI gains automatically offset pressure on the core business.

That tension explains the SaaSpocalypse debate. The original fear, triggered in February when new AI agent tools hit software valuations, was seat compression and automation of routine services. The September quarter shows clients paying Indian firms to do the integration work instead. It does not show that pricing pressure has ended.

What happens next

The next test is arithmetic over several quarters: can AI revenue, growing at 19% to 29% per quarter from a 10% base, outgrow the deflation in the other 90% of the business? Deal wins, hiring for AI and cloud roles, and whether Wipro and Tech Mahindra begin disclosing AI revenue — Tech Mahindra has said it plans to in the second half of FY27 — will give investors a fuller picture.

For Indian professionals in the diaspora, the direction is clearer than the destination. Demand is shifting from headcount-based delivery toward AI implementation skills, and the firms that were priced as AI's first casualties are, for now, being paid to build it.
